Q: How to add non-standard (linker) flag (e.g. containing a whitespace) to SCons? A:

If the flags are standalone, and multi-word, use a list (or tuple) of strings when Appending, or enter them using the --opt=option-arg form if your tool will accept that, avoiding the space problem. I believe emcc will accept this? Life gets more complicated if the flags have to stay together with something SCons needs to treat differently - that was the problem in the linked question.

Q: DIFFERENCE returns 1 at an INT32 counter rollover while DIFF returns -4294967295 A:

As per documentation:

  • DIFFERENCE outputs a result of the same type of the operands
  • DIFF outputs a result of type DOUBLE

The difference in sign is given because with INT32 the difference between the two numbers (respectively maximum and minimum INT32 value) causes an overflow, while DOUBLE is represented with more bits thus, it doesn't overflow showing the real result.

Q: NativeScript vs. Flutter A:

Flutter is not the main deal here, the real thing is Skia.

skia is a 2d rendering engine which allows the user to run apps in high performance, this way instead of using html(chrome web engine) or using the native look and feel(nativescript) skia allows us to draw on each pixel of the screen, which allows us to write games in flutter.

Google real intentions as they reviled in flutter Live 2018 are to create a coherent UI between all platforms:

  • desktop
  • web (hummingbird)
  • mobile (flutter)

all of those frameworks use skia for UI and the respective framework for interacting with the OS (browser, desktop, mobile), because skia is a rendering engine and we control every pixel we can assure that a widget will look the same on all type of skia frameworks.

On the other hand nativescript use a node engine which they load on the platform, and each time we try to use a component we call the system engine to place a component on the screen with the native look and feel, this allows us to use features straight from the virtual machine which runs java/swift, this is why in nativescript you can use android.[ANDROID_JAVA_CLASS] or ios.[SWIFT_CLASS].

nativescript main invention is around using native classes from inside nodejs engine which they are loading on runtime in-order to execute the specific platform code. When you are transforming nativescript mobile code to a PWA there is no need for this node engine because the browser has it's own engine this way we can remove unnecessary code from the PWA.

NOTE: nativescript is not an angular framework for mobile development its a nodejs framework for mobile development and Angular/vuejs are just frameworks which runs on top of nativescript core logic. Thats why if you want you can even write a react plugin for nativescript.

Q: Unable to import matplotlib pyplot A:

hope you're doing good.

If you want to just use pyplot, do this.

Use pip to manage packages
pip install matplotlib

Next the way you import is much outdated nowadays, even though it's correct.
It should be like;
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

This way you can access the sub-module aka pyplot when writing code.

Btw, pip is already there if you have python installed. So no need to install it separately.

Q: Issue in detecting the bubble of OMR sheet A:

Here is one way to do that in Python OpenCV.

(Since you did not provide your original image, I have to start with your thresholded image)

  • Read the input image

  • Crop to remove extraneous white pixels along the borders

  • Convert to grayscale (gray), then create a version as float in the range 0 to 1 (gray2), then create a 3 channel version (gray3) from gray

  • Threshold gray (as thresh), then create another thresholded version (thresh2) as float in range 0 to 1

  • Get external contours from thresh

  • Create a mask image initialized to black from gray2. This will be used later to find the mean values inside each contour.

  • Set up constants for threshold tests to be use subsequently

  • Compute and save the centers of all contours that are larger than a threshold value. Also compute the masked mean values from gray2 for each contour

  • Align x and y values to their mean values from the saved centers to form unique column and row x and y values. That is form grids lines.

  • Compute and print the number of rows and columns

  • Compute row and column indices

  • Save table 1 with original center x,y values for the found answers, i.e. the filled-in bubbles (circles) in the OMR image

  • Save table 2 with original center values and the indices of the columns and rows for the found answers in the OMR image, i.e., x,y,column_idx,row_idx

  • Draw the contours on the 3-channel gray3 image

  • Print table 1

  • Bring table 2

Input image:

Cropped Image:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# Read the input image
img = cv2.imread('OMR3.png')

# Crop the image to remove white borders
img2 = img[45:45+620, 2:251]

# Convert to grayscale
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img2, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# Normalize gray image to a float range of 0.0 to 1.0
if gray.max() > 1:
    gray2 = gray.astype(np.float32) / 255.0
else:
    gray2 = gray.copy().astype(np.float32)

# Convert gray to a 3 channel version gray3
gray3 = cv2.cvtColor(gray, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR)

# Threshold gray image and create version thresh2 in float range (0.0 to 1.0)
thresh = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)[1]
thresh2 = thresh.astype(np.float32) / 255.0

# Get contours from the thresh image
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_NONE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]


# Initialize a mask filled with zeros (black)
mask = np.zeros(gray2.shape[:2], dtype=np.uint8)

# Define threshold value and gap tolerance values
threshold_value = 0.5  # values greater than this for the mean become "found answers"
fraction = 0.4  # multiplies the median gap as the tolerance
min_tolerance = 5
fallback_tolerance = 10

# Compute and save the centers of all contours and their masked means from gray2 
# that that are larger than a threshold value
detected_data = []
for contour in contours:
    mask[:] = 0
    cv2.drawContours(mask, [contour], -1, 255, -1)
    
    mean_val = cv2.mean(gray2, mask=mask)[0]
    
    if mean_val > threshold_value:
        M = cv2.moments(contour)
        if M["m00"] != 0:
            cX = int(M["m10"] / M["m00"])
            cY = int(M["m01"] / M["m00"])
        else:
            cX, cY = 0, 0
        detected_data.append({'contour': contour, 'x': cX, 'y': cY, 'mean': mean_val})

# Align x and y values to their mean values from the save centers to form unique 
# column and row x and y values. That is form grids lines.
def cluster_coordinates_auto(coords):
    # Find x or y values as provided in coords that are not too close 
    # according to the max between the min allowed gap, i.e, min_tolerance and the 
    # median gap multiplied by fraction. Put clustered coords into a unique list 
    # (cluster in a list of clusters ). Each cluster contains all x or y coordinates,
    # that are close enough to each other. Returns the mean of each cluster of x or y

    # Sort the list of x or y coordinates as provided from smallest to largest
    sorted_coords = sorted(coords)
    if not sorted_coords:
        return []
    
    # Calculate the differences between adjacent x or y coordinates as provided
    diffs = np.diff(sorted_coords)
    
    # Trap for 1 point, i.e. 0 pairs, then return the original sorted x or y 
    # since the list contains only 1 point.
    if len(diffs) == 0:
        return [int(sorted_coords[0])]
    
    # Filter out zero or near-zero differences as coordinates are too close
    non_zero_diffs = [d for d in diffs if d > 1]
    
    if non_zero_diffs:
        # Use a fraction of the median gap (distance) between distinct x or y as the tolerance.
        # Typically, the gap between coordinates is much larger than the jitter of coordinates.
        tolerance = max(min_tolerance, int(np.median(non_zero_diffs) * fraction))
    else:
        tolerance = fallback_tolerance  # Fallback default

    # clusters is a list of lists of similar sorted x or y coordinates
    # Each sub-list contains all similar x or y values
    # clusters[-1] is the last sub-list of x or y coordinate in the "clusters" 
    # of sorted x or y coordinates.
    # clusters[-1][-1] is the last x or y coordinated in the last (previous) cluster 
    # and is used for the tolerance test.
    # first -1 gets the last cluster (the active one) and the second -1 gets the 
    # last x or y in that cluster
    clusters = [[sorted_coords[0]]]  # list of lists of one item the first (x or y)
    for val in sorted_coords[1:]: # gets the second sorted x or y coordinate
        if val - clusters[-1][-1] <= tolerance:
        # Append to the current cluster if within the tolerance
            clusters[-1].append(val)
        else:
            clusters.append([val])
    # Returns a single value from the mean of each cluster of x or y coordinates  
    # that are clustered because they have similar values
    return [int(np.mean(c)) for c in clusters]

# Separates x and y values from the detected x and y coordinates that pass 
# the threshold test into their own lists    
all_x = [item['x'] for item in detected_data]
all_y = [item['y'] for item in detected_data]

# Clusters the x and y mean coordinates from each cluster that pass 
# the tolerance test in order to compute a regular grid of x and y.
# grid_x_lines and grid_y_lines are a list of mean x or y coordinates 
# from each cluster 
grid_x_lines = cluster_coordinates_auto(all_x)
grid_y_lines = cluster_coordinates_auto(all_y)

# Compute the number of rows and columns in the grid 
num_cols = len(grid_x_lines)
num_rows = len(grid_y_lines)

print(f"\nDetected Grid Structure: {num_rows} rows x {num_cols} columns\n")

# Computes row and column indices on a regular grid from abs difference 
# between cluster x or y and the actual x or y coordinates.
table1_rows = []
table2_rows = []

for item in detected_data:
    
    # Get the actual x and y from the threshold passed coordinates
    orig_x, orig_y = item['x'], item['y']
    
    # Find closest grid column and row index (as 1-based indices).
    # Loop over actual (orig_x or orig_y), then loop over every grid line and 
    # measure its distance to a given orig_x or orig_y. Then compute the row or  
    # column index of the grid line that is closest to the selected orig_x or orig_y. 
    col_idx = min(range(len(grid_x_lines)), key=lambda i: abs(grid_x_lines[i] - orig_x)) + 1
    row_idx = min(range(len(grid_y_lines)), key=lambda i: abs(grid_y_lines[i] - orig_y)) + 1
    
    # Create table 1 that only stores [x, y]
    table1_rows.append([orig_x, orig_y])
    
    # Create table 2 that stores [x, y, col_idx, row_idx]
    table2_rows.append([orig_x, orig_y, col_idx, row_idx])
    
    # Draw red contours for found answers on the gray3 image
    cv2.drawContours(gray3, [item['contour']], -1, (0, 0, 255), 2)

# Sort table 2 entries by column index first, then row index
table2_rows.sort(key=lambda item: (item[2], item[3]))

# Print a list of Found Answer centers, i.e. found filled-in circles
print("\n--- TABLE 1: List of Found Answer Centers ---")
print(f"{'Center X':<8} {'Center Y':<8}")
print("-" * 18)
for x, y in table1_rows:
    print(f"{x:<8} {y:<8}")

# Print a list of Found Answer centers & Row/Column Indices
print("\n\n--- TABLE 2: Table of Found Answer Centers and Column/Row Indices ---")
print(f"{'Center X':<8} {'Center Y':<8} {'Col Index':<10} {'Row Index':<10}")
# print row of 18 dashes
print("-" * 38)
for x, y, col, row in table2_rows:
    print(f"{x:<8} {y:<8} {col:<10} {row:<10}")   

# Print counts of all contours and those that passed the mean test.
print(f"\n\nCount of All Contours:", len(contours))
print(f"Total Number of Found Answers: {len(table2_rows)}\n")

# save and show results
cv2.imwrite('omr3_cropped.png', img2)
cv2.imwrite('omr3_thresh.png', thresh)
cv2.imwrite('omr3_contours.png', gray3)

cv2.imshow("cropped", img2)
cv2.imshow("thresh", thresh)
cv2.imshow("contours", gray3)

cv2.waitKey(0)
cv2.destroyAllWindows()
